Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures . ' Measure ' is another name for an upgrade or retrofit that can be applied to a building.

An ' end-use savings shape ' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1 Technology Summary

This work evaluates a reference case where existing space heating and air conditioning equipment in homes with existing ductwork is upgraded to the minimum efficiency available (circa 2025) ⎯ or like-for-like replacements for above-minimum equipment -across the U.S. residential building stock. The purpose of this reference case is to provide a comparison point for other measures and packages that simulate heating and cooling equipment replacements at the end of the equipment 's useful life (also called 'at wear out'). This enables estimates of incremental energy savings and incremental upfront cost of measures compared to an assumed alternative.

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

Fuel-fired furnaces -including propane, fuel oil, and natural gas -are used to heat indoor environments. Fuel ignites in the burner, and the flame heats a metal heat exchanger. A blower fan moves air over the heat exchangers, which warms the air. Most furnaces use ducts to distribute heat, while combustion exhaust is vented outside. In comparison, gravity furnaces do exist but are older and not as common; as such in this study, we only model forced air furnaces.

Fuel-fired wall or floor furnaces are directly installed within walls or floors to serve one or a few rooms. They burn natural gas, propane, or fuel oil in a combustion chamber, transferring heat through a heat exchanger. Heated air rises by convection into occupied spaces, and combustion byproducts should be vented outside the dwelling. Unlike central furnaces, they typically do not use ducts and instead provide localized heating.

Electric furnaces use resistance heating elements rather than combustion to produce heat. When an electric current passes through the elements, they generate heat, which is transferred to air moving across them. A blower fan distributes this heated air through ducts.

to produce heat. When an electric current passes through the elements, they generate heat, which is transferred to air moving across them. A blower fan distributes this heated air through ducts.

Fuel boilers heat water instead of air. Natural gas, propane, or fuel oil is burned in a combustion chamber to heat water. The hot water (or steam in some systems) is then circulated through pipes to radiators, baseboard heaters, or radiant floor systems. Boilers can provide both space heating and domestic hot water. Combustion gases are vented outside the building.

Central air conditioners typically use the same duct network as the heating system. They remove heat from buildings by operating a vapor-compression cycle: an outdoor unit compresses and condenses refrigerant, which then absorbs heat from indoor air as it passes over an evaporator coil. A blower fan circulates the cooled air through the ducts, and the absorbed heat is expelled outdoors; system efficiency is measured by the seasonal energy efficiency ratio, version 2 (SEER2), with higher ratings indicating more efficient cooling.

the ducts, and the absorbed heat is expelled outdoors; system efficiency is measured by the seasonal energy efficiency ratio, version 2 (SEER2), with higher ratings indicating more efficient cooling.

Room air conditioners are self-contained cooling units designed to cool a single room or small area. They are typically mounted in windows or through walls and operate using a vaporcompression cycle: they draw in warm indoor air, cool it by passing it over the evaporator coil, return it to the room, and expel heat outside. Room air conditioners are rated by their combined energy efficiency ratio (CEER).

Air-source heat pumps (ASHPs) provide both heating and cooling using a reversible vaporcompression cycle. In cooling mode, they operate like a central air conditioner, transferring heat from indoors to outdoors, but in heating mode, the cycle reverses and they extract heat from outdoor air and deliver it indoors. Even at cold temperatures, heat pumps can capture usable energy from the outdoor air. Distribution is typically through the same duct network used for cooling, though ductless systems deliver conditioned air directly to rooms. Efficiency is rated using heating seasonal performance factor, version 2 (HSPF2) for heating and SEER2 for cooling.

Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.2  Sizing

HVAC sizing is automatic across all HVAC system types and sizes following the ACCA Manual J/S methodology. ACCA Manual J (ACCA, 2024) provides guidelines for calculating the design heating and cooling loads in a building, and ACCA Manual S (ACCA, 2014) provides a guide for selecting the size of residential HVAC systems to meet those loads. For a full description of sizing and system selection for ASHPs, reference the Dual Fuel Heat Pump System documentation (White et al. 2025).

Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3  Efficiency

Efficiency is rated using annual fuel utilization efficiency (AFUE) for natural gas furnaces, SEER2 for air conditioning systems, HSPF2 for heat pumps, CEER for room air conditioners. Importantly, SEER2 and HSPF2 include fan energy but AFUE does not.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3.1 Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency

AFUE is the standard rated efficiency for how efficiently a furnace converts fuel into heat at rated conditions. The higher the AFUE rating, the more efficient the system is at converting fuel into usable heat. Energy lost through exhaust gases, radiation, and other components decreases efficiency.

AFUE is the total annual heat output divided by the total annual fuel input -on a scale of 0% to 100%. Note that unlike SEER2 and HSPF2, AFUE does not include the electricity used by the air handler blower, combustion blower, ignition system, or controls. ANSI/ASHRAE 103-2022 provides a procedure for determining AFUE of residential central furnaces and boilers, which is a test cycle structured to simulate ordinary heating conditions throughout the year -including seasons (ANSI/ASHRAE 2022).

' Residential furnaces manufactured and distributed in commerce, as defined by 42 U.S.C. 6291(16) must meet the energy conservation standards specified in the Code of Federal Regulations at 10 CFR 430.32 ' (DOE 2025b). 80% AFUE furnaces are the minimum for nonweatherized gas furnaces (i.e., natural gas and propane) manufactured from 2015 through Dec. 18, 2028. After Dec. 18, 2028, the minimum is 95% AFUE. If an investigator would like to understand equipment standard changes over time, a useful approach could blend data from this study with data from the Propane and Fuel Oil Furnaces upgrade (Stenger et al. 2026b) as well as the Natural Gas Furnaces upgrade (Stenger et al. 2026a), both of which model 95% AFUE for propane and natural gas furnaces, respectively. In this study, we model an 80% AFUE as minimum efficiency natural gas furnace when existing efficiency is rated lower than 80% AFUE, and a like-for-like replacement when the existing natural gas furnace is rated above 80% AFUE.

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3.2  Combined Energy Efficiency Ratio

CEER is the standard rated efficiency for room air conditioners under specific test conditions. It measures how effectively the unit converts electrical energy into cooling capacity; the higher the CEER rating, the more efficient the system.

CEER is defined as the ratio of the steady-state cooling capacity (i.e., Btu/hr) to the electrical power input (i.e., kW) under rated conditions (Code of Federal Regulations 2025). Because it is measured at a single set of conditions, energy efficiency ratio (EER) provides a snapshot of performance rather than a seasonal metric. For portable and room air conditioners, CEER accounts for standby and off-mode power consumption, but has different test procedures.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3.3 Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, Version 2

SEER2 is a metric for representing the cooling efficiency of central air conditioners and heat pumps as they would perform over an entire cooling season. It is defined as the total cooling output (in British thermal units, Btu) during a typical cooling season divided by the total electrical energy input, including the blower fan energy (in watt-hours) consumed over that same period. Higher SEER2 values indicate more efficient systems, since they deliver more cooling per unit of electricity. Energy losses due to on-off cycling, blower waste heat, and refrigerant line heat transfer all reduce SEER2.

SEER2 is determined under standardized test conditions specified by ANSI/AHRI Standard 210/240-2024 (and DOE's Appendix M1), which simulates a range of outdoor temperatures and indoor loads to approximate real-world operation throughout the cooling season. Ratings typically range from about 13 SEER2 for older equipment up to 26 SEER2 for more advanced centrally ducted air-conditioner systems, and up to 35.1 SEER2 for non-ducted systems.

In this study, dwellings with existing air-conditioning systems below the regional minimums are modeled with central air conditioners or heat pumps rated at 14.3 SEER2 in the South region and 13.4 SEER2 in the North region, and with central ASHPs rated at 14.3 SEER2 and 7.5 HSPF2. The South region includes the following states: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawai ' i, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Nevada, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, and the District of Columbia. text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3.4  Heating Seasonal Performance Factor, Version 2

HSPF2 is a rating representing the heating efficiency of heat pumps as they perform over an entire heating season. It is defined as the total heating output (in Btu) during a typical heating season divided by the total electrical energy input, including the energy consumed by the indoor blower fan (in watt-hours) and outdoor unit over that same period. Higher HSPF2 indicates more efficient systems, since they deliver more heating per unit of electricity. Factors such as on-off cycling, coil defrost cycles, and standby power consumption can reduce HSPF2.

HSPF2 is determined under standardized test conditions, which simulate a range of outdoor temperature and part-load conditions to approximate real-world performance throughout the heating season. Residential central air conditioning heat pumps manufactured and distributed in commerce, as defined by 42 U.S.C. 6291(16), must meet the energy conservation standards specified in the Code of Federal Regulations at 10 CFR 420.32(c)(5) (DOE 2025a).

In this study, dwellings with existing systems below the regional minimums are modeled with ducted heat pumps rated at 7.5 HSPF2. For dwellings whose current heating equipment already meets or exceeds these thresholds, we simulate a like-for-like replacement at the higher efficiency.

This upgrade replaces space heating and cooling equipment in homes with existing ductwork with units that meet minimum efficiency standards reflective of circa-2025 requirements. It includes:

- Replacement of non-ducted electric resistance heating systems (boiler, baseboard, wall furnace) with baseline 100% efficiency electric options for costing consistency.

In homes that have existing ductwork that is used for heating but not central air conditioning, the non-ducted air conditioning systems are also replaced:

Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 3 Modeling Approach

This section outlines how the upgrade is modeled in ResStock using the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow. In this scenario, dwellings meeting the applicability logic receive the upgrade. ResStock uses probabilistic sampling logic based on national housing stock data to assign each dwelling unit a set of baseline building characteristics, including existing heating fuel, system type, and duct configuration. Ducts remain unchanged when heating and cooling systems are upgraded, which can yield inefficiencies. The model assumes consistent operation patterns across households and scales furnace capacity based on heating load requirements determined by building envelope characteristics and climate zone. While equipment brand and installation quality are not modeled explicitly, the total heating energy demand and fuel consumption are recalculated to reflect the standardized furnace and fuel use. This scenario represents a reference case where all space heating and air conditioning equipment is upgraded to the minimum efficiency available (or like-for-like replacements for above-minimum equipment) across the U.S. residential building stock. The purpose of this reference case is to provide a comparison point for other measures and packages that simulate heating and cooling equipment replacements at the end of the equipment's useful life (also called 'at wear out'). This enables estimates of inc
